claim: Naturalistic animal behavior exhibits variability arising from at least three sources: hierarchical, contextual, and stochastic.
source: Naturalistic animal behavior exhibits a strikingly complex organization in the temporal domain, with variability arising from at least three sources: hierarchical, contextual, and stochastic.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational premise of the review.

claim: Naturalistic animal behavior exhibits a striking amount of variability in the temporal domain.
source: Naturalistic animal behavior exhibits a striking amount of variability in the temporal domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A which illustrates the three sources of temporal variability.

claim: Behavioral action sequences arrange in a hierarchical structure where actions are nested into behavioral sequences that are then grouped into activities.
source: A leading theory to explain the temporal organization of naturalistic behavior is that behavioral action sequences arrange in a hierarchical structure (Tinbergen, 1951; Dawkins, 1976; Simon, 1962), where actions are nested into behavioral sequences that are then grouped into activities.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational theoretical work.

claim: This hierarchy of timescales is ubiquitously observed across species during naturalistic behavior.
source: This hierarchy of timescales is ubiquitously observed across species during naturalistic behavior.
evidence: This is stated as an established observation in the field.

claim: Reaction times are faster when stimuli are expected compared to when stimuli are unexpected.
source: For example, reaction times to a delivered stimulus can be consistently faster when an animals is expecting it compared to slower reaction times when the stimulus is unexpected (Jaramillo and Zador, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: The distribution of movement durations is typically very skewed with an exponential tail.
source: This residual variability across repetitions can be quantified as a property of the distribution of movement durations, which is typically very skewed with an exponential tail (Wiltschko et al., 2015; Findley et al., 2021; Recanatesi et al., 2022), suggesting a stochastic origin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies that measured movement duration distributions.

claim: Variability in movement execution may originate from noise in force production within muscles.
source: Variability in movement execution and body posture (Dhawale et al., 2017) may originate from the motor periphery, such as noise in force production within muscles (van Beers et al., 2004), or from the deterministic chaotic dynamics arising from neural activity (Costa et al., 2021) or the biomechanical structure of an animal's body (Loveless et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies investigating sources of motor variability.

claim: Metastable attractors are emerging as a unifying principle for explaining many different aspects of the dynamics and function of neural circuits.
source: The mechanistic approach we will review is based on the theory of metastable attractors (Figure 1B), which is emerging as a unifying principle expounding many different aspects of the dynamics and function of neural circuits (La Camera et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1B illustrating the concept.

claim: Transitions between metastable attractors can be driven by neural variability internally generated within a local recurrent circuit.
source: Our starting point is the observation that transitions between metastable attractors can be driven by the neural variability internally generated within a local recurrent circuit.
evidence: This is stated as a foundational observation for the mechanistic theory being reviewed.

claim: The average transition time between metastable attractors can be regulated by changes in single-cell gain.
source: We will show that the average transition time between metastable attractors can be regulated by changes in single-cell gain.
evidence: This is stated as a finding that will be demonstrated in the review.

claim: A large hierarchy of timescales can naturally and robustly emerge from heterogeneities in a circuit's structural connectivity motifs, such as neural clusters with heterogeneous sizes.
source: Finally, we will review how a large hierarchy of timescales can naturally and robustly emerge from heterogeneities in a circuit's structural connectivity motifs, such as neural clusters with heterogeneous sizes.
evidence: This is stated as a finding that will be reviewed in the manuscript.

claim: Computational methods for animal pose tracking have recently undergone a revolution due to spectacular accuracy and efficiency.
source: The study of naturalistic behavior based on animal videos has recently undergone a revolution due to the spectacular accuracy and efficiency of computational methods for animal pose tracking (Stephens et al., 2008; Berman et al., 2014; Hong et al., 2015; Mathis et al., 2018; Pereira et al., 2019; Nourizonoz et al., 2020; Segalin et al., 2020); see Appendix 1 and Table 1 for details).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent methodological advances.

claim: New computational methods for pose tracking work across species and conditions.
source: These new methods work across species and conditions, ushering a new era for computational neuroethology (Anderson and Perona, 2014; Brown and de Bivort, 2018; Datta et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles on computational neuroethology.

claim: Transition times between consecutive actions are well described by a Poisson process.
source: At the timescale of actions and postures, transition times between consecutive actions are well described by a Poisson process (Killeen and Fetterman, 1988), characterized by a right-skewed distribution of inter-action intervals (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 3 showing the distribution.

claim: State-space models fail to account for longer timescale and non-Markovian structure in behavior.
source: However, these models fail to account for longer timescale and non-Markovian structure in behavior, and in later sections we will move to a more data-driven approach to investigate these aspects of behavior (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of state-space models.

claim: The secondary motor cortex (M2) in rodents is part of a distributed network involved in motor planning in head-fixed mice.
source: A large number of studies implicated the secondary motor cortex (M2) in rodents as part of a distributed network involved in motor planning in head-fixed mice (Li et al., 2016; Barthas and Kwan, 2017) and controlling the timing of self-initiated actions in freely moving rats (Murakami et al., 2014; Murakami et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Ensemble activity recorded in M2 during the Marshmallow task unfolded via sequences of multineuron-firing patterns, each one lasting hundreds of milliseconds to a few seconds.
source: Ensemble activity recorded in M2 during the Marshmallow task unfolded via sequences of multineuron-firing patterns, each one lasting hundreds of milliseconds to a few seconds; within each pattern, neurons fired at an approximately constant rate (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3B showing the neural data.

claim: The onset of specific neural patterns reliably preceded upcoming self-initiated actions.
source: A dictionary between actions and neural pattern could be established, revealing that the onset of specific patterns reliably preceded upcoming self-initiated actions (Figure 3A and B;e.g., the onset of the red pattern reliably precedes the poke out movement).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3A and B showing the correspondence.

claim: Neural patterns in M2 may represent attractors of the underlying recurrent circuit dynamics.
source: Neural patterns in M2 may represent attractors of the underlying recurrent circuit dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the observed neural dynamics.

claim: An attractor is a persisting pattern of population activity where neurons fire at an approximately constant rate for an extended period of time.
source: Within the context of neural activity, an attractor is a persisting pattern of population activity where neurons fire at an approximately constant rate for an extended period of time (see Appendix 1 for models of attractor dynamics).
evidence: This is a definition provided in the text.

claim: Licking preparatory activity in M2 during a delayed response task is encoded by choice-specific discrete attractors.
source: Foundational work in head-fixed mice showed that licking preparatory activity in M2 during a delayed response task is encoded by choice-specific discrete attractors (Inagaki et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Attractors can be stable, as observed in monkey IT cortex in working memory tasks.
source: Attractors can be stable (Amit and Brunel, 1997), as observed in monkey IT cortex in working memory tasks (Fuster and Jervey, 1981; Miyashita and Chang, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental and theoretical work.

claim: Metastable attractors typically last for hundreds of milliseconds and noise fluctuations spontaneously trigger transitions to a different attractor.
source: Attractors can also be metastable (see Appendix 3), when they typically last for hundreds of milliseconds and noise fluctuations spontaneously trigger transitions to a different attractor (Deco and Hugues, 2012; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical modeling work.

claim: M2 ensemble activity in the Marshmallow experiment was consistent with the activity generated by a specific sequence of metastable attractors.
source: In particular, M2 ensemble activity in the Marshmallow experiment was consistent with the activity generated by a specific sequence of metastable attractors (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3 showing the model and data.

claim: The onset of an attractor drives the initiation of a specific action as determined by the action/pattern dictionary.
source: The main hypothesis underlying this model is that the onset of an attractor drives the initiation of a specific action as determined by the action/pattern dictionary (Figure 3A and B) and the dwell time in a given attractor sets the inter-action-interval.
evidence: This is stated as the main hypothesis of the model.

claim: The main features observed in the M2 ensemble dynamics can be explained by a two-area mesoscopic network where a large recurrent circuit representing M2 is reciprocally connected to a small circuit lacking recurrent couplings.
source: The main features observed in the M2 ensemble dynamics during the Marshmallow task (i.e., long-lived patterns with a right-skewed dwell-time distribution, concatenated into highly reliable pattern sequences) can be explained by a two-area mesoscopic network where a large recurrent circuit (representing M2) is reciprocally connected to a small circuit lacking recurrent couplings (a subcortical area likely representing the thalamus [Guo et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2017; Inagaki et al., 2022], see Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work and reference to Figure 5C showing the model.

claim: Transitions between consecutive attractors are driven by low-dimensional noise fluctuations arising in the feedback projections from the subcortical nucleus back to M2.
source: In this biologically plausible model, metastable attractors are encoded in the M2 recurrent couplings, and transitions between consecutive attractors are driven by low-dimensional noise fluctuations arising in the feedback projections from the subcortical nucleus back to M2.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the proposed model.

claim: The distribution of dwell times for each attractor is right-skewed as a consequence of the stochastic origin of the transitions.
source: As a consequence of the stochastic origin of the transitions, the distribution of dwell times for each attractor is right-skewed, closely matching the empirical data.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction of the model that matches empirical observations.

claim: Ensemble fluctuations around each pattern were found to be low-dimensional and oriented in the direction of the next pattern in the sequence.
source: This model's prediction was confirmed in the data, where the ensemble fluctuations around each pattern were found to be low-dimensional and oriented in the direction of the next pattern in the sequence (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3 showing the data analysis.

claim: Low-dimensional correlations in motor circuits are essential for motor generation during naturalistic behavior.
source: This model presents a new interpretation for low-dimensional (differential) correlations: although their presence in sensory cortex may be detrimental to sensory encoding (Moreno-Bote et al., 2014), their presence in motor circuits seems to be essential for motor generation during naturalistic behavior (Recanatesi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations contrasting findings in sensory and motor cortex.

claim: A causal test of the hypothesis that preparatory activity for upcoming actions is encoded in discrete attractors in M2 in freely moving animals is currently lacking.
source: Although it is not possible to measure potential wells directly in the brain, using mean field theory one can show that the height of these potential wells is directly proportional to the neuronal gain as measured by single-cell transfer functions (for an explanation, see Appendix 3).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the current literature.

claim: The height of potential wells is directly proportional to the neuronal gain as measured by single-cell transfer functions.
source: Although it is not possible to measure potential wells directly in the brain, using mean field theory one can show that the height of these potential wells is directly proportional to the neuronal gain as measured by single-cell transfer functions (for an explanation, see Appendix 3).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical result from mean field theory.

claim: A decrease in pyramidal cells gain can lead to faster average action timing.
source: In particular, a decrease (increase) in pyramidal cells gain can lead to faster (slower) average action timing.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the theoretical model.

claim: Valid expectations accelerated reaction times and improved detection accuracy in an auditory two-alternative choice task.
source: When manipulating the expectations about sound timing, valid expectations accelerated reaction times and improved detection accuracy, showing enhanced perception.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding from the cited study.

claim: The auditory cortex is necessary to perform the auditory discrimination task.
source: The auditory cortex is necessary to perform this task, and firing rates in auditory cortex populations are modulated by temporal expectations.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claim: Optogenetic activation of serotonergic neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus selectively prolonged the waiting period in the self-initiated waiting task.
source: In the self-initiated waiting task of Figure 3A, optogenetic activation of serotonergic neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus selectively prolonged the waiting period, leading to a more patient and less impulsive behavior, but did not affect the timing of other self-initiated actions (Fonseca et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: After a rewarded trial, mice exhibited longer latency to initiate the next trial, but shorter press durations.
source: After a rewarded trial, mice exhibited longer latency to initiate the next trial, but shorter press durations; after a failure, the opposite behavior occurred, with shorter latency to engage and longer press durations.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation from the cited study.

claim: Trial history effects rely on frontal areas such as medial prefrontal and secondary motor cortices.
source: Inactivation experiments showed that these effects rely on frontal areas such as medial prefrontal and secondary motor cortices (Murakami et al., 2014; Murakami et al., 2017; Schreiner et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to inactivation experiments.

claim: Changes in baseline levels modulate the average transition times between metastable attractors.
source: In a recurrent circuit exhibiting attractor dynamics, changes in baseline levels modulate the average transition times between metastable attractors (Mazzucato et al., 2019; Wyrick and Mazzucato, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical modeling work.

claim: Changes in input baseline that decrease the barrier height lead to faster transitions to the coding attractor.
source: Changes in input baseline that decrease (increase) the barrier height lead to faster (slower) transitions to the coding attractor, in turn modulating reaction times.
evidence: This is stated as a mechanism from the theoretical model.

claim: This biologically plausible computational mechanism was proposed to explain the acceleration of sensory coding observed when gustatory stimuli are expected compared to when they are delivered as a surprise.
source: This biologically plausible computational mechanism was proposed to explain the acceleration of sensory coding observed when gustatory stimuli are expected compared to when they are delivered as a surprise (Samuelsen et al., 2012; Mazzucato et al., 2019); and the faster encoding of visual stimuli observed in V1 populations during locomotion periods compared to when the mouse sits still (Wyrick and Mazzucato, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental and modeling work.

claim: Gain modulation is a general mechanism to flexibly control network activity in recurrent network models of motor cortex.
source: Theoretical work has established gain modulation as a general mechanism to flexibly control network activity in recurrent network models of motor cortex (Stroud et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to theoretical work.

claim: Individual modulation of each neuron's gain can allow a recurrent network to learn a variety of target outputs through reward-based training.
source: Individual modulation of each neuron's gain can allow a recurrent network to learn a variety of target outputs through reward-based training and combine learned modulatory gain patterns to generate new movements.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the cited theoretical work.

claim: A comparison of monocular and binocular mice revealed different visually guided strategies mice may use to perform a successful jump.
source: For example, in a distance estimation task where mice were trained to jump across a variable gap, a comparison of monocular and binocular mice revealed the different visually guided strategies mice may use to perform a successful jump.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claim: Mice performed more vertical head movements under monocular conditions compared to control, revealing a reliance on motion parallax cues.
source: Mice performed more vertical head movements under monocular conditions compared to control (Figure 5A, states 2 and 3 occur more frequently in the monocular condition), revealing a reliance on motion parallax cues (Parker et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 5A showing the data.

claim: Experimentally controlled manipulations can lead to strong changes in ongoing behavior reflected both in changes of state usage and of transition probabilities between actions.
source: Experimentally controlled manipulations can lead to strong changes in ongoing behavior reflected both in changes of state usage and of transition probabilities between actions, resulting in different repertoires of behavioral sequences.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation from experimental studies.

claim: A classification analysis predicted with high accuracy which drug and specific dose was administered to mice from a large panel of compounds at multiple doses.
source: In the latter study, a classification analysis predicted with high accuracy which drug and specific dose was administered to the mice from a large panel of compounds at multiple doses.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the cited study.

claim: In a model of sequence generation, the basal ganglia sequentially disinhibit motif-specific thalamic units, which in turn trigger motif preparation and execution via a thalamocortical loop with the primary motor cortex.
source: In this model (Figure 5B), the basal ganglia sequentially disinhibit motif-specific thalamic units, which in turn trigger motif preparation and execution via a thalamocortical loop with the primary motor cortex (M1).
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the cited model and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Sequential activity patterns can be learned in an all-inhibitory circuit representing the striatum based on biologically plausible synaptic plasticity rules.
source: Within the framework of corticostriatal circuits, sequential activity patterns can be learned in an all-inhibitory circuit representing the striatum (Murray and Escola, 2017). Learning in this model is based on biologically plausible synaptic plasticity rules, consistent with the decoupling of learning and execution suggested by lesion studies showing that cortical circuits are necessary for learning, but that subcortical circuits are sufficient for expression of learned behaviors (Kawai et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling and experimental work.

claim: The combination of fast cortical learning and slow subcortical learning may give rise to a covert learning process through which control of behavior is gradually transferred from cortical to subcortical circuits.
source: The combination of fast cortical learning and slow subcortical learning may give rise to a covert learning process through which control of behavior is gradually transferred from cortical to subcortical circuits, while protecting learned behaviors that are practiced repeatedly against overwriting by future learning.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the cited theoretical work.

claim: In the Marshmallow task about 10% of the temporal variability in waiting times could be attributed to a trial history effect.
source: For example, in the Marshmallow task about 10% of the temporal variability in waiting times could be attributed to a trial history effect, which relied on an intact medial prefrontal cortex and was abolished with its inactivation (Murakami et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: The remaining 90% of the unexplained across-repetition variability was attributed to a stochastic mechanism, likely originating from metastable dynamics.
source: The remaining 90% of the unexplained across-repetition variability was attributed to a stochastic mechanism, likely originating from metastable dynamics (Recanatesi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to modeling work.

claim: The worm locomotor behavior exhibits a clear hierarchical organization with three distinct timescales: sub-second body-bends and head-casts, second-long crawling undulations, and slow reverse-forward cycles.
source: The worm locomotor behavior exhibits a clear hierarchical organization with three distinct timescales: sub-second body-bends and head-casts, second-long crawling undulations, and slow reverse-forward cycles (Gomez-Marin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: At the neuronal level, the hierarchy in C. elegans is generated by nested neuronal dynamics where upper-level motor programs are supported by slow activity spread across many neurons, while lower-level behaviors are represented by fast local dynamics in small multifunctional populations.
source: At the neuronal level, this hierarchy is generated by nested neuronal dynamics where upper-level motor programs are supported by slow activity spread across many neurons, while lower-level behaviors are represented by fast local dynamics in small multifunctional populations (Kaplan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Persistent activity driving higher-level behaviors gates faster activity driving lower-level behaviors in C. elegans.
source: Persistent activity driving higher-level behaviors gates faster activity driving lower-level behaviors, such that, at lower levels, neurons show dynamics spanning multiple timescales simultaneously (Hallinen et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: The motor hierarchy in C. elegans has a nonoverlapping, tree-like structure, in which no lower-level state is connected to multiple upper-level states.
source: Specific lower-level behaviors may only be accessed via switches at upper levels, generating a nonoverlapping, tree-like hierarchy, in which no lower-level state is connected to multiple upper-level states.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the C. elegans motor hierarchy.

claim: The state-level hierarchy in C. elegans may rely on neuromodulation.
source: Whereas the motor hierarchy is directly generated by neuronal activity, this state-level hierarchy may rely on neuromodulation (Ben Arous et al., 2009; Flavell et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Berman et al. mapped the entire behavioral space of freely moving flies, identifying a hundred stereotyped, frequently reoccurring actions, interspersed with bouts of nonstereotyped behaviors.
source: By analyzing videos of ground-based fruit fly during long sessions of spontaneous behavior (Figure 2B), Berman et al., 2014 and Berman et al., 2016 mapped the entire behavioral space of freely moving flies, identifying a hundred stereotyped, frequently reoccurring actions, interspersed with bouts of nonstereotyped behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the cited studies.

claim: The information bottleneck method revealed multiple timescales in the fly behavior, organized into a hierarchical structure reflecting the underlying behavioral programs and internal states.
source: This predictive algorithm revealed multiple timescales in the fly behavior, organized into a hierarchical structure reflecting the underlying behavioral programs and internal states.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from applying the information bottleneck method.

claim: A strongly non-Markovian structure emerges on longer timescales in fly behavior.
source: These longer timescales manifest as nested blocks in the transition probability matrix, implying that a strongly non-Markovian structure emerges on longer timescales (Alba et al., 2020; Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 7A.

claim: The different branches of the fly behavioral hierarchy are segregated into a tree-like, nonoverlapping structure.
source: A hallmark of the fly behavior emerging from this analysis is that the different branches of this hierarchy are segregated into a tree-like, nonoverlapping structure: for example, actions occurring during grooming do not occur during locomotion.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding from the analysis of fly behavior.

claim: Optogenetic activation of single descending neurons in the fly drove stereotyped behaviors that were shared by multiple neurons and often depended on the behavioral state prior to activation.
source: Optogenetic activation of single neurons during spontaneous behavior revealed that most of the descending neurons drove stereotyped behaviors that where shared by multiple neurons and often depended on the behavioral state prior to activation (Cande et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Individual flies vary considerably in the high-level temporal structure of locomotion, and in how this usage is modulated by different odors.
source: An alternative statistical approach based on a hierarchical HMM revealed that, although all flies use the same set of low-level locomotor features, individual flies vary considerably in the high-level temporal structure of locomotion, and in how this usage is modulated by different odors (Tao et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Behavioral idiosyncrasy of individual-to-individual phenotypic variability has been traced back to specific genes regulating neural activity in the central complex of the fly brain.
source: This behavioral idiosyncrasy of individual-to-individual phenotypic variability has been traced back to specific genes (Ayroles et al., 2014) regulating neural activity (Buchanan et al., 2015) in the central complex of the fly brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Mice acquired the 'penguin dance' sequence hierarchically rather than sequentially, a learning scheme that is inconsistent with the classic reinforcement learning paradigm.
source: Mice acquired the sequence hierarchically rather than sequentially, a learning scheme that is inconsistent with the classic reinforcement learning paradigm, which predicts sequence learning occurs in the reverse order of execution (Sutton and Barto, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding that contradicts a theoretical prediction.

claim: Striatal direct and indirect pathways play differential roles in controlling the expression of a single action or a fast switch from one subsequence to the next.
source: Using closed-loop optogenetic stimulation, the authors revealed the differential roles played by striatal direct and indirect pathways in controlling, respectively, the expression of a single action (either L or R), or a fast switch from one subsequence to the next (from the LL block to RR, and from RR to the reward approach).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding from optogenetic manipulation.

claim: Signature of non-Markovian dynamics in rat behavior peaked at 10–100 s timescales.
source: Examining the behavioral transition matrix at different timescales, signature of non-Markovian dynamics peaked at 10–100 s timescales.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis of rat behavior.

claim: On 15 s timescales, pattern sequences emerged featuring sequentially ordered actions, such as grooming sequences of the face followed by the body.
source: On 15 s timescales, pattern sequences emerged featuring sequentially ordered actions, such as grooming sequences of the face followed by the body.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis of rat behavior.

claim: On minute-long timescales, states of varying arousal or task engagement emerged, lacking stereotyped sequential ordering.
source: On minute-long timescales, states of varying arousal or task engagement emerged, lacking stereotyped sequential ordering.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis of rat behavior.

claim: In a rat model of the fragile X syndrome, mutant rats showed abnormally long grooming epochs, characterized by different behavioral sequences and states compared to wildtypes.
source: In a rat model of the fragile X syndrome, while mutant and wildtype rats had similar locomotor behavior, the former showed abnormally long grooming epochs, characterized by different behavioral sequences and states compared to wildtypes (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 7C showing the data.

claim: Differences between individual rats were more pronounced at longer timescales compared to short ones.
source: Another benefit of this multiscale approach is to allow the investigation of the individuality of rodent behavior, revealing that, although all animals drew from a common set of temporal patterns, differences between individual rats were more pronounced at longer timescales compared to short ones (Marshall et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: A heterogeneous distribution of timescales of neural activity was found in the brainstem of the restrained larval zebrafish by measuring the decay time constant of persistent firing.
source: A heterogeneous distribution of timescales of neural activity was found in the brainstem of the restrained larval zebrafish by measuring the decay time constant of persistent firing across a population of neurons comprising the oculomotor velocity-to-position neural integrator (Figure 8A; Miri et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 8A.

claim: The decay times varied over a vast range 0.5–50 s across cells in individual zebrafish larvae.
source: The decay times varied over a vast range 0.5–50 s across cells in individual larvae.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from the cited study.

claim: This heterogeneous distribution of timescales was confirmed in the primate oculomotor brainstem.
source: This heterogeneous distribution of timescales was later confirmed in the primate oculomotor brainstem (Joshua et al., 2013), suggesting that timescale heterogeneity is a common feature of oculomotor integrators conserved across phylogeny.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Temporal traces of the reward delivered in previous trials were encoded in single-neuron spiking activity in frontal areas over a wide range of timescales, obeying a power law distribution up to 10 consecutive trials.
source: In head-fixed monkeys performing a competitive game task, temporal traces of the reward delivered in previous trials were encoded in single-neuron spiking activity in frontal areas over a wide range of timescales, obeying a power law distribution up to 10 consecutive trials (Bernacchia et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: The distribution of intrinsic autocorrelation timescales within the same cortical circuit was found to be right-skewed and approximately lognormal, in the range from 10 ms to 1 s.
source: In awake head-fixed primates, during periods of ongoing activity, the distribution of intrinsic autocorrelation timescales within the same cortical circuit was found to be right-skewed and approximately lognormal (Figure 8B), in the range from 10 ms to 1 s (Cavanagh et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 8B.

claim: Comparison of the population-averaged autocorrelations during ongoing periods revealed a hierarchical structure across cortical areas, varying from 50 to 350 ms along the occipital-to-frontal axis.
source: Moreover, comparison of the population-averaged autocorrelations during ongoing periods revealed a hierarchical structure across cortical areas, varying from 50 to 350 ms along the occipital-to-frontal axis (Murray et al., 2014; Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 8C.

claim: Current evidence from freely moving rodents engaged in waiting tasks revealed the presence of multiple timescales in single-neuron activity from secondary motor and prefrontal cortices.
source: While all these results were obtained in restrained animals, it is an open question whether neural activity during naturalistic behavior exhibits temporal hierarchies similar to those observed in behavior. Current evidence from freely moving rodents engaged in waiting tasks (Murakami et al., 2017; Schreiner et al., 2021; Recanatesi et al., 2022) revealed the presence of multiple timescales in single-neuron activity from secondary motor and prefrontal cortices.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: These timescales range from the sub-second scale (single attractors), to a few seconds (attractor sequences), to tens of seconds or minutes (trial history dependence).
source: These timescales range from the sub-second scale (single attractors), to a few seconds (attractor sequences), to tens of seconds or minutes (trial history dependence).
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of the timescales observed in the cited studies.

claim: Population activity in hippocampal CA1 and CA3 encodes multiplexed information about several aspects of the task occurring on multiple trials such as context, place, value, and objects.
source: Evidence from associative learning tasks in rodents found that population activity in hippocampal CA1 and CA3 encodes multiplexed information about several aspects of the task occurring on multiple trials such as context, place, value, and objects (McKenzie et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Single-cell biophysical properties such as differences in membrane time constant across cell types or synaptic time constants across receptors may generate multiple timescales in sub-second range.
source: Single-cell biophysical properties such as differences in membrane time constant across cell types or synaptic time constants across receptors (e.g., faster AMPA and GABA vs. slower NMDA receptors) may generate multiple timescales in sub-second range, from a few milliseconds to a few hundred milliseconds (Gjorgjieva et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to theoretical work.

claim: Recurrent networks with random recurrent couplings can generate time-varying neural activity whose timescale may be tuned to very slow values at a critical point.
source: Recurrent networks with random recurrent couplings can generate time-varying neural activity whose timescale may be tuned to very slow values at a critical point (Toyoizumi and Abbott, 2011; Magnasco et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Long timescales may also emerge in random neural networks with an excess of symmetric couplings.
source: Long timescales may also emerge in random neural networks with an excess of symmetric couplings (Martí et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to theoretical work.

claim: Two biologically plausible ingredients were shown to be sufficient to generate long timescales with temporal heterogeneity in their distributions: recurrent couplings realizing local functional neural clusters and heterogeneity in synaptic couplings.
source: Two biologically plausible ingredients were shown to be sufficient to generate long timescales with temporal heterogeneity in their distributions: recurrent couplings realizing local functional neural clusters and heterogeneity in synaptic couplings.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical finding.

claim: The strength of recurrent couplings decays with spatial distance between pairs of neurons, leading to the emergence of local functional assemblies of strongly coupled neurons.
source: The first requirement of functional assemblies is a connectivity motif ubiquitously observed in biological circuits, namely, the fact that the strength of recurrent couplings decays with spatial distance between pairs of neurons, leading to the emergence of local functional assemblies of strongly coupled neurons (Song et al., 2005; Perin et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2016; Kiani et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental work.

claim: Linear networks featuring both local functional assemblies and spatial heterogeneity in long-range couplings were able to reproduce the heterogeneous decay times found in the brainstem oculomotor integrator circuit in zebrafish and primates.
source: Linear networks featuring both local functional assemblies and spatial heterogeneity in long-range couplings were able to reproduce the heterogeneous decay times found in the brainstem oculomotor integrator circuit in zebrafish and primates (Miri et al., 2011; Joshua et al., 2013) and in the reward integration times in the macaque cortex (Bernacchia et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling work that reproduced experimental findings.

claim: In a model based on excitatory and inhibitory neurons arranged in clusters of heterogeneous sizes, a cluster's timescale is proportional to its size and larger clusters exhibit longer timescales.
source: In this model, a cluster's timescale is proportional to its size and larger clusters exhibit longer timescales, yielding a heterogeneous distribution of timescales in the range observed in cortex (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the model described in the cited work.

claim: No study to date investigated the presence of temporal hierarchies in neural activity during naturalistic behavior.
source: First, although temporally heterogeneous neural activity was found in several brain areas and species under different experimental conditions, no study to date investigated the presence of temporal hierarchies in neural activity during naturalistic behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the current literature.

claim: Recent advances in neurotechnology demonstrate the feasibility of chronic recordings of large neural populations during freely moving behavior.
source: All the necessary tools are available: recent advances in neurotechnology demonstrate the feasibility of chronic recordings of large neural populations during freely moving behavior (Juavinett et al., 2019; van Daal et al., 2021); simultaneously performing behavioral classification analyses from pose tracking software (Mathis et al., 2018; Marshall et al., 2021; Pereira et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent methodological advances.

claim: Self-initiated actions within a behavioral sequence are represented as metastable attractors in secondary motor cortex.
source: We start from the observation that self-initiated actions within a behavioral sequence are represented as metastable attractors in secondary motor cortex (Inagaki et al., 2019; Recanatesi et al., 2022; Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Behavioral units at each level of the temporal hierarchy (actions, sequences, activities) are represented by metastable attractors.
source: We then extend this observation to a general principle positing that behavioral units at each level of the temporal hierarchy (not only actions, but also sequences, activities) are represented by metastable attractors.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed general principle extending from experimental observations.

claim: The stochasticity in behavioral unit duration can be achieved by generating transitions between attractors at each level via low-dimensional variability, arising from mesoscopic feedback loops involving cortex and subcortical areas.
source: The stochasticity in behavioral unit duration can be achieved by generating transitions between attractors at each level via low-dimensional variability, arising from mesoscopic feedback loops involving cortex and subcortical areas (Recanatesi et al., 2022; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism supported by a citation.

claim: The average transition time between behavioral units at each level depends on the barrier height separating the corresponding attractors.
source: The average transition time between behavioral units at each level will then depend on the barrier height separating the corresponding attractors (Cao et al., 2016; Mazzucato et al., 2019; Wyrick and Mazzucato, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: As one moves up the hierarchy from actions to sequences to activities, the potential wells separating the corresponding attractors become deeper and the basins of attraction wider.
source: As one moves up the hierarchy from actions (fast transitions = lower barriers) to sequences and activities (slow transitions = higher barriers), the potential wells separating the corresponding attractors become deeper and the basins of attraction wider.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the proposed hierarchical model.

claim: This increase in timescales can be achieved in a biological manner by assuming that increasingly larger neural populations encode for slower behavioral features.
source: This increase in timescales can be achieved in a biological manner by assuming that increasingly larger neural populations encode for slower behavioral features (Stern et al., 2021; see Figure 8E), which can be realized in a biologically plausible way as a hierarchy of clusters within clusters (Schaub et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Contextual modulations in average duration of a behavioral unit at each level of the hierarchy can be implemented by top-down changes of the barrier heights between attractors via gain modulation.
source: Contextual modulations in average duration of a behavioral unit at each level of the hierarchy can be implemented by top-down changes of the barrier heights between attractors via gain modulation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism.

claim: Neurons exhibit conjunctive selectivity to multiple variables at different levels of the hierarchy.
source: First, neurons exhibit conjunctive selectivity to multiple variables at different levels of the hierarchy, which has been observed, for example, in rodent hippocampus during freely moving tasks (McKenzie et al., 2014) and in primate prefrontal cortex during complex decision-making tasks (Rigotti et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Single-cell activity is modulated by many attractors, in agreement with the multistable activity observed in sensory and frontal areas.
source: Second, single-cell activity is modulated by many attractors, in agreement with the multistable activity observed in sensory (Mazzucato et al., 2015) and frontal areas (Recanatesi et al., 2022) where neuronal representations of attractors are dense rather than sparse.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Fluctuations in the activity of single neurons should vary over multiple timescales simultaneously, encoding information about multiple levels of the hierarchy.
source: Third, fluctuations in the activity of single neurons should vary over multiple timescales simultaneously, encoding information about multiple levels of the hierarchy; this is the structure that was observed in C. elegans where neurons representing movements exhibit both fast and for slow fluctuations correlated to multiple levels of the behavioral hierarchy (Kaplan et al., 2020; Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated as a prediction that is supported by observations in C. elegans.

claim: The behavioral hierarchy discovered in flies can be approximated as a tree where behavioral units at a lower level of the hierarchy only occur during a specific unit at a higher level of the hierarchy.
source: The behavioral hierarchy discovered in flies (Berman et al., 2016) can be approximated as a tree: behavioral units at a lower level of the hierarchy only occur during a specific unit at a higher level of the hierarchy (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of the fly behavioral hierarchy.

claim: Movements occurring during the fruit fly locomotion activities never occur during idle activities.
source: For example, movements occurring during the fruit fly locomotion activities never occur during idle activities.
evidence: This is stated as an example of the tree-like structure.

claim: A classic model of hierarchical attractors is an extension of the Hopfield network where the stored pattern is hierarchically arranged into a tree.
source: A classic model of hierarchical attractors, which could potentially capture the tree-based hierarchy, is an extension of the Hopfield network where the stored pattern is hierarchically arranged into a tree (Parga and Virasoro, 1986; Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to theoretical work.

claim: This class of models was originally proposed to explain the effect of word semantic categorization during memory encoding, storage, and retrieval.
source: This class of models was originally proposed to explain the effect of word semantic categorization during memory encoding, storage, and retrieval.
evidence: This is stated as the original application of the model.

claim: The results of Marshall et al., 2021 suggest that the hierarchy in rats may not be tree-like as the one observed in flies.
source: It is still an open question to determine the precise structure of the behavioral hierarchy in mammals. The results of Marshall et al., 2021 seem to suggest that the hierarchy in rats may not be tree-like as the one observed in flies (Berman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of experimental findings.

claim: The mammalian hierarchical motor system may allow for flexible and adaptable behaviors, by utilizing the same motor elements across different sequences in a hierarchical manner.
source: On general grounds, it would be interesting to investigate whether the mammalian hierarchical motor system allows for flexible and adaptable behaviors, by utilizing the same motor elements across different sequences in a hierarchical manner, as represented in the mesoscopic circuit models of Murray and Escola, 2017; Logiaco and Escola, 2020; Logiaco et al., 2021 (see Figure 5) and suggested by experimental evidence in Geddes et al., 2018.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by citations to modeling and experimental work.

claim: In the cortico–thalamic–basal ganglia model, flexible sequences can be generated by rearranging existing motifs as well as by learning new motifs without interfering with previous ones.
source: In the cortico–thalamic–basal ganglia model of Figure 5B, flexible sequences can be generated by rearranging existing motifs as well as by learning new motifs without interfering with previous ones (Logiaco et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to modeling work.

claim: Flexible sequences can be learned using biologically plausible Hebbian plasticity in the striatum.
source: Moreover, flexible sequences can be learned using biologically plausible Hebbian plasticity in the striatum (Murray and Escola, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to modeling work.

claim: At the lowest level of the hierarchy, neural populations in the rodent secondary motor cortex (M2) generate metastable attractors representing upcoming actions.
source: In the case of mammals, at the lowest level of the hierarchy, neural populations in the rodent secondary motor cortex (M2) generate metastable attractors representing upcoming actions (Inagaki et al., 2019; Recanatesi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Other subcortical areas, such as the basal ganglia or the thalamus, are likely involved in the generation of complex behavioral sequences.
source: Other subcortical areas, such as the basal ganglia or the thalamus, are likely involved in the generation of complex behavioral sequences (Murray and Escola, 2017; Logiaco et al., 2021; Recanatesi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling and experimental work.

claim: Single neurons in M2 are selective to multiple actions, suggesting that mixed selectivity could play an important role in generating the high-dimensional hierarchical attractor landscape necessary to capture the complexity of naturalistic behavior.
source: Experimental evidence shows that single neurons in M2 are selective to multiple actions (Recanatesi et al., 2022), suggesting that mixed selectivity (Rigotti et al., 2013) could play an important role in generating the high-dimensional hierarchical attractor landscape necessary to capture the complexity of naturalistic behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work and theoretical concepts.

claim: While behavioral units are encoded as cortical attractors, transitions between attractor rely on feedback loops involving cortico–subcortical circuits.
source: In both scenarios, we hypothesize that while behavioral units are encoded as cortical attractors, transitions between attractor rely on feedback loops involving cortico–subcortical circuits (Murray and Escola, 2017; Logiaco et al., 2021; Recanatesi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by citations to modeling work.

claim: During courtship, a male fly can simultaneously approach a female fly (locomotion) and sing, two behaviors that would be mutually exclusive in the absence of a female fly.
source: For example, during courtship, a male fly can simultaneously approach a female fly (locomotion) and sing, two behaviors that would be mutually exclusive in the absence of a female fly.
evidence: This is stated as an example of multitasking during social behavior.

claim: The simple tree-like hierarchical organization of behavior observed in isolated individuals might break down during social interactions and lead to a flexible organization where actions are shared between multiple sequences and activities.
source: As a consequence, the simple tree-like hierarchical organization of behavior observed in isolated individuals (Figure 8) might break down during social interactions and lead to a flexible organization where actions are shared between multiple sequences and activities.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis about how social interactions may change behavioral organization.
